column1: In drumming, what is the fundamental principle governing rebound control?
column2: Drumming is energy transfer, not muscle force — the head stores kinetic energy on impact and releases it back into the stick; grip should be loose enough to let rebound happen but firm enough to redirect it.

column1: What happens when a drummer uses a choked (too tight) grip on impact?
column2: The grip absorbs the returning energy in the fingers instead of letting it re-launch the stick, producing a 'dead' stop at the head instead of rebound.

column1: In matched grip, which two fingers form the fulcrum, and what is their job?
column2: Thumb and index finger pad form the fulcrum; they do the steering of the stick, while middle, ring, and pinky close gently to catch the rebound and reopen to let it fly.

column1: Where should the fulcrum be positioned relative to the stick's balance point?
column2: Forward of the balance point, toward the tip — approximately 1.5 inches (about four finger-widths) forward of the balance mark.

column1: Approximately how far from the butt end does a drumstick's natural balance point fall on a standard 5A/5B stick?
column2: About 5–7 cm (2–3 inches) from the butt end, or roughly 40–45% up from the butt end.

column1: What is the approximate tempo threshold above which wrist motion alone can no longer keep up with 16th-note rebound control?
column2: Roughly 140 BPM (140–160 BPM) of 16th notes — above this, fingers must take over rebound control or the hands will lock up.

column1: In the 'kinetic chain' model of drumming, what distinct role does each of forearm, wrist, and fingers play?
column2: Forearm: gross positioning/power for accents (rotation). Wrist: primary engine for strokes below ~140 BPM sixteenths (flexion/extension, like a loose hinge). Fingers: fine control, catching rebound, adding late 'whip' speed, and executing doubles/buzz strokes.

column1: Using the 'transmission' analogy, what are the wrist and fingers each compared to, and what is the consequence of relying on only one?
column2: Wrist = engine, fingers = clutch and throttle. Wrist-only playing hits a speed ceiling around 140–160 BPM sixteenths; finger-only playing has no power behind it.

column1: Approximately what percentage of impact velocity does a well-tuned drumhead return to the stick as rebound?
column2: 60–80% of the impact velocity is returned as rebound.

column1: How does stroke volume relate to impact velocity in drumming physics?
column2: Stroke volume tracks impact velocity, but acoustic energy scales roughly with the square of velocity — doubling stick speed roughly quadruples the acoustic energy.

column1: What is the practical target grip pressure for the thumb-index fulcrum when gripping a stick (if measured on a scale)?
column2: Roughly half a pound, about 220–250 grams, measured with thumb and index only.

column1: Why is mentally subdividing the beat down to the 16th-note (or finer) grid important for a drummer, even when playing quarter notes?
column2: It lets the drummer place ghost notes, flams, and syncopations exactly where they belong rather than approximating them — this constant internal subdivision is what makes playing feel 'locked in'.
